_comment_family: Telegraf ships as a family of cuts that all carry 'Telegraf' as name
ID 1 — the UltraLight in this folder and the UltraBold beside it are
two files answering to one family name, separated only by their
subfamily. Asking for 'Telegraf' alone would let either of them
answer, and these two are at opposite ends of the weight axis: a
title measured against the hairline and drawn in the ultra bold does
not merely look different, it overflows the block.
So the full name (name ID 4) is what gets declared, the same way
The two Telegraf packs are therefore two faces with two distinct
family names, which is also what lets one channel be set in both at
once (see `highlight.face` in js/channels.js): fontguard keys its
check by family, so each cut is verified in its own right.
_comment_css: Not declared in styles.css: this face arrived with a channel and is
registered from this JSON, which is the route content/README.md
describes. Nothing has to be added to the stylesheet for it.
_comment_local: What the machine may already know the face by, tried after the file.
The first is the PostScript name and is also what the installer
registers the face under; the second is the Windows full name. Both
name this one cut rather than the family, so a machine answering to
either is answering with this file — which is exactly what the
fallback route is for. 'Telegraf' on its own is deliberately absent:
it is the name the UltraBold answers to as well.
_comment_stack: The fallbacks are damage limitation and never a design choice — a
title laid out against the wrong metrics is broken, not merely
different, which is what fontguard exists to catch before it is ever
drawn. They are still chosen rather than copied: every other face in
this folder falls back through Impact and Arial Black because every
other face here is a heavy display cut, and putting a 200-weight
hairline behind Impact would make the one thing that survives a
missing file the furthest possible thing from it. Segoe UI Light is
on every Windows this app runs on and is the nearest weight the
machine can be relied on to have.
